brief.head: Blame the state
brief.text: Monopolies do not arise in a free market with proper competition, Amit Varma argued. They come from state interference shielding a crony, or from the state itself. {060-C06}

brief.head: Resist easy wins
brief.text: Big problems are slow and hard to credit, so many researchers retreat to small ones they can solve. Amit Varma’s advice to the young: keep your eye on the target. {060-C10}

brief.head: The CEO as superstar
brief.text: We credit a superstar CEO like Jack Welch for what a dispersed organisation achieved, Amit Varma said, and we make the same mistake with heads of government. {060-C14}

brief.head: A day is your life
brief.text: Grand goals are toxic, Amit Varma said: achieve one and grander ones appear. A day is not a waiting room for life to happen. A day is your life. {060-C16}

brief.head: Not a restaurant
brief.text: At a restaurant everyone orders what they like. In a democracy, outvoted diners eat seafood or go hungry. Hence, Amit Varma said, the need for a republic. {060-C19}

thought.text: Thinking is precious, is always precious.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why states aren’t firms
lead.head: A firm hand, the wrong job
body: Amit Varma opened with a “light triad” to set against the dark triad of serial killers: three words beginning with F. They were firms, finance and freedom. {060-J01}

Firms, both hosts agree, are awesome. That is the trouble. It is a short step to thinking that someone who has run a good firm, or advised one, could run a country better than “random extra politicians”.
“That is a terrible, terrible fallacy,” Varma said, born of a top-down instinct from our hunter-gatherer past.
The episode drew on a chapter of *In Service of the Republic*, by Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah: a country is not a company.
“At the end, gentle reader, we hope to persuade you that the two skills are really completely apart,” Shah said. {060-C01}
He borrowed a friend’s analogy: firms are cells, and the economy is the organism. There is no prosperity without healthy firms, but what works for a cell does not work for the body.
## Counting the ways
First, feedback. A firm sees its stock price daily, its production weekly and its profits monthly, so mistakes show up within months.

Government has no such scorecard: the stock index says little about the economy, and GDP comes quarterly and late. “Firms can work well and have a better chance at working well because there are feedback loops and they get slapped into shape,” Shah said. {060-C03}

Second, survival. A firm can go bankrupt; a ministry cannot. “If you are the defence ministry of India, you are the defence ministry of India,” Shah said. “You could lose wars, many things could go wrong, but basically your life is assured.”
Third, coercion. A firm is a raft of voluntary contracts. The state holds a monopoly of violence; it is, Shah said, “a coercive creature”.
Fourth, complexity. Shah, who knows both worlds, finds firms clean and solvable beside government’s tangle of departments and objectives.
Fifth, rules. A small firm can hustle from deal to deal, but a state that bargains with each citizen offers “rule of men”, not rule of law, and “the pathway to infinite corruption”. {060-C12}
Sixth, power. A small firm can be run by one boss; a state must split power between branches and between layers of government.

Seventh, time. India, Shah said, is on a hundred-year journey to close a 9x gap with America in per capita GDP. Every reform must pass through a policy pipeline that is, in his word, inexorable. {060-C15}
## Business is not banned

None of this makes business people unfit to govern, Varma insisted. Flexible thinkers such as Paul Graham, Naval Ravikant or Jeff Bezos could change how they think. The “standard issue McKinsey consultant”, he added, was another matter.
Nor are politicians natural governors. Many master the game of retail politics, Varma said, then find that governance and policy are different games altogether.

Shah, a great admirer of what India’s firms have achieved since the early nineties, called their best people world class. But their skills, he warned, do not transfer straight into public policy. Varma named the bias: the halo effect.

Shah’s book of the day, *When McKinsey Comes to Town* by Walt Bogdanich and Michael Forsythe, came with a caution: “the book is a bit mean, it’s a bit one-sided.” Still, he said, it shows how hard it is to bring a consulting approach to the complex problems of public policy.

second.label: Social science
second.head: A penny in a stormy pool
second.deck: Amit Varma on why governments cannot run clean experiments
body: Social science is not like the physical sciences, Amit Varma said, and he had an analogy from his friend Shruti Rajagopalan, who may have had it from Don Boudreaux. In a laboratory, testing whether a coin displaces water is easy: measure a beaker, drop the coin in gently, measure again.
Now try it in a crowded swimming pool, a hundred metres by a hundred, with a storm overhead and forty people swimming and throwing things. Everything is multicausal. {060-C04}

A business choosing between two blends of polyester can run an A/B test and tinker its way to an answer, Varma said. {#polyester} A government is in the pool, and is not even sure what it is measuring.

quote.text: There is a storm overhead, there are forty people swimming inside and throwing things, and you’re trying to drop a coin there.

second.caption: the coin in the stormy pool

third.head: Catastrophe, then a rally
body: COVID was a terrible catastrophe, Ajay Shah said. Yet when the US Fed and the RBI cut rates sharply, stock prices went up. {060-S01}
Firms were not suddenly being run better. “It was really about a new interest rate for computing NPVs,” he said: the same future profits, discounted at a lower rate.

So nobody, he said, should mistake the stock market index for a report card on the economy or the government. Stock prices are not “non informative nonsense”: there is a lot of sense in what they do. They simply do not report the health of the economy.
That leaves a country without the daily scorecard a firm enjoys. In public policy, Shah said, “It’s a little bit of flying blind.” {#blind}
third.caption: the COVID stock rally

p2.title: Poles apart
p2.deck: Seven ways a state is not a firm, from a chapter of *In Service of the Republic* {060-R01}

sections.label: First difference
sections.head: The feedback that never comes
sections.caption: feedback loops
body: A firm lives inside a loop of information, Ajay Shah said. It watches its market share, its revenue, its profits and its stock price, which comes out daily. When something goes wrong, management hears about it within months.
So a firm need not be run by a big thinker. It can debug its way forward, solving one small problem after another. That does not produce great leaps, Shah said, but it keeps the firm going.

Government has no such loop. GDP, at its best, is a quarterly number with a considerable lag, and in India its measurement has run into many difficulties. Mistakes can “perpetuate damage week after week and month after month”. In government, Shah said, there are no such feedback loops. {060-C03}
## Votes are not verdicts
Elections, he added, come once every five years and are only mildly related to performance, and base passions still weigh disproportionately in winning them. {#elections}
Amit Varma saw the opposite problem: with state and local polls always round the corner, elections are in effect happening all the time, and they drive short-termism.

Even the signal voters send can point the wrong way. Agriculture needs deep structural change, which takes years and cannot quickly be credited to anyone. A farm loan waiver wins votes now, and has become a hygiene factor that everybody offers.
~ Sometimes, Varma conceded, distress is so great that a waiver is needed. But it is an anaesthetic, not a cure.

quote.text: A waiver like that can be a necessary anaesthetic, but it is not the structural change you need.

sections.label: Second and third
sections.head: The ministry that cannot die
sections.caption: monopoly and coercion
body: In a private firm, Ajay Shah said, bankruptcy is always on the table. A ministry has no such worry: even a defence ministry that loses wars is assured of its life. {060-C05}
For many state bodies, he said, monopoly means not supernormal profits but unquestioned coercive power, and without the fear of death comes complacence.

Amit Varma went further. In a free market with proper competition, he said, a monopoly is impossible. Monopolies come from state interference that shields a crony, or from the state itself, with its monopolies on violence and money. {060-C06}
Market failure, he added, is incredibly rare. Government failure is ubiquitous.
## A raft of contracts

A firm, Shah said, is a set of voluntary contracts with customers, employees and other firms. The few that hire gundas are scummy, and their people belong in jail. The state, in Max Weber’s definition, holds a monopoly of physical violence in a territory. {060-C07}
Varma added the double thank you, John Stossel’s phrase for a voluntary exchange that leaves both people better off. The state has no need to earn a thank you: it takes what it wants. {060-C08}
~ The same person, Varma said, faces very different incentives at the head of a firm and at the head of a government. As Lord Acton said, power corrupts. {060-J13}

quote.text: That to be the state is to have coercive power.

sections.label: Fourth difference
sections.head: Shoot first, think later?
sections.caption: complexity and the bias for action
body: Even a large firm is simple next to government, Ajay Shah said, which spreads across many departments and offices, with different objectives, each pulling its own way.
Having worked in both worlds, he finds firms clean and solvable, and government so complicated that you must scale back even the ambition of measuring and understanding it. {060-C09}
## A bias for action?

That led to the episode’s open disagreement. Shah has grown uncomfortable with a favourite slogan of startups and venture capital, a bias for action, even in business. Shooting first and asking questions later is superficial, he said, and in government “truly dangerous”. {060-C11}
Policy needs thought first: what is the market failure, what is the lowest-cost intervention, and how will it reshape incentives and survive the political economy?

Amit Varma agreed about the state. About firms, he said, “I can’t disagree more strongly with that.” Great companies start out doing one thing, then iterate and pivot, a lesson he drew partly from the essays of Paul Graham. {060-R06}
They agreed it is not a binary. Jeff Bezos, Varma said, had a bias for action and was also a deep thinker. Shah’s real target, he suggested, was reflexive short-termism.
~ Varma invited viewers to ask for a full episode on the question, though Shah, he joked, might decline: “That will be bias for action.” {060-J05}

quote.text: Whereas with government, it is like, my God, this is too hard. This is impossibly complicated.

sections.label: Fifth difference
sections.head: No haggling with the state
sections.caption: rules versus deals
body: A firm may live from deal to deal, Ajay Shah said. It can agree to deliver nickel of a certain grade for six months at a certain price, delivery point Shanghai. {#nickel}

Government cannot work that way. Its many arms need policy coherence across time and across organisations, or one will contradict another. And a state that strikes deals with private persons offers rule of men, not rule of law. {060-C12}
Its job, Shah said, is to set stable rules that reshape incentives, so that private people can make long-term plans. It should not be making steel or a payment system.
## The franchise lesson

Large firms discover rules too. McDonald’s could strike a different deal with every franchisee, since no Article 14 binds it to equal treatment. In practice it offers a standard contract, or it would fall apart in complexity and corruption. {#mcdonalds}
The state, the most complex organisation of all, is bound by Article 14. It cannot give one citizen one deal and another a different one.
Shah had little patience for talk of a China model, in which a Fortune 500 chief flies in to shake hands with a strongman. That, he said, should embarrass us. {060-J03}
~ Amit Varma added that firms adopt rules as they scale, from Six Sigma to Google’s motto of “do no evil”.

quote.text: The engagement between a government and a private person can absolutely not be deals.

sections.label: Sixth difference
sections.head: Octopus beats starfish
sections.caption: the dispersion of power
body: In a five-man firm, Ajay Shah said, the CEO can be “a little demigod” while the others cower. But past any meaningful scale, a firm run by one person telling everybody what to do is guaranteed to be mediocre.

A friend gave him an image for this. A tiny firm is like cooking: the cook chooses garlic or onions. A growing one is gardening, where you create conditions, culture and incentives, and run a portfolio of bets. {#gardening}
In a country as diverse as India, he added, even a firm should not be a starfish with one brain at the centre, but an octopus, with thinking people all over. {#starfish}
## No choice for the state
For the state, Shah said, there is no option: the only way known to make a government work is to disperse power. {060-C13}

So the state is split into legislative, executive and judicial branches, and into a union government, “a little confused creature called a state government”, and city or village governments. {060-J04}
An autocratic firm, Amit Varma noted, costs society little: there will be fifty other firms, and it learns or dies. {#fifty}
~ Subsidiarity, Shah said, follows from the same idea: each city knows best what it should do for itself.

quote.text: There’s a single big insight in two thousand years of politics and political philosophy, it is this one sentence, dispersion of power.

sections.label: Seventh difference
sections.head: The hundred-year game
sections.caption: time horizons
body: In India, Ajay Shah said, an underdeveloped financial system makes the cost of capital very high. Put a high rate into a net present value calculation and the future is really not there, so firms are inevitably short-sighted.
Many in the private sector, he said, don’t care about five years out, because they will have sold the company to the next buyer within three years. {#threeyears}
Government must play a longer game. India is on a hundred-year journey to close a 9x gap with America in per capita GDP. {#gap}
## Down the pipeline

Reform, Shah said, runs through a pipeline: data and research, theories of change, a lively public debate, expert committees, the drafting of laws, and then state capacity, with process manuals and training. {060-C15}
It takes 10 to 20 years to make a material difference in any field, a rhythm most of the private sector is not used to. {#pipeline}

Amit Varma brought the frame home. Think about life over the longest horizon, he said, and live it over the shortest, because life is a succession of days. He quoted Annie Dillard: “How you spend your days is, of course, how you spend your life.” {060-J19}
~ He used to make the mistake, he said, of fixing on awards to win and books to write.

quote.text: There is a policy pipeline and it is inexorable. It is a damn pipeline.

side.boxText: The episode follows a chapter of *In Service of the Republic*, by Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah. All the points are made there, Amit Varma said, “beautifully written”. The video is a companion: “but please read.” {#chapter}

contQuote.text: It’s not enough to be a democracy. You need to be a republic where you have a constitution protecting the people from the state, not the other way around.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Judgment withheld, a puzzle solved, two rules and a test

stories.start: in the past on this show I mentioned Alice Monroe's short stories
stories.end: inside her head or inside the heads of all the people concerned
stories.caption: Alice Munro
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a writer he loves and a story he can’t judge
stories.head: The other stories we don’t know
body: Amit Varma has spoken on the show before about Alice Munro’s short stories and what she means to him. Then the news broke. {060-R05}

Munro’s daughter had said that her mother’s second husband abused her when she was nine, and that Munro turned a blind eye and did nothing. For people who love her work, Varma said, it brought complicated emotions. Some people rushed to judgment.
Before his flight to DC, where he was recording episodes, his friend Shruti Rajagopalan messaged him. She is a Munro fan too, and she was disturbed. So was he.
On the plane he read David Brooks’s *How to Know a Person*, a book that echoed what Varma had learned from long-form podcasting about listening and long conversations. {060-R03}

Brooks writes about Vivian Gornick’s *Fierce Attachments*, in which Gornick and her mother live almost at cross purposes, understanding each other completely, and yet not at all. He uses it to show the complexity of human beings, and why we should not always jump to judgment.

On the flight, Varma decided. He would keep loving Munro’s work and withhold judgment on her. “Because the world is too complex,” he said. “We know one story. We don’t know the other story. We don’t know the other stories.” {060-S05}

~ He was clear that Munro, in minimising her daughter’s grief, did something “clearly wrong at many levels”. And while he separates art from artist, there are writers, like Pablo Neruda, he will never read “because I know too much about them”. {060-J20}
stories.why: Most of the time we know only one version of a messy human story. Withholding judgment, without excusing what was wrong, can be wiser than a rush to condemn or defend.
stories.postscript: It does not matter much either way, Varma added: Munro is gone, and “it’s not like I’m having dinner with her”.

stories.start: this reminds me of a quiz question I had once set in a quiz
stories.end: So millihelen is the beauty that will launch one ship.
stories.caption: the Warhol, a unit of hype
stories.kicker: Amit Varma sets a puzzle, and Ajay Shah does the sums
stories.head: Fifteen minutes, by arithmetic
body: Talk of celebrity culture reminded Amit Varma of a question he had set at a quiz about 15 years ago. A good quiz question, he said, is one where you can work out the answer. {060-S03}
He read it out to Ajay Shah. “X is a unit of hype. One kilo X is equal to 10.42 days. One mega X is equal to 28.5 years. What is X?” {060-J11}

Shah worked aloud: 0.01 days, about 864 seconds. Twelve minutes, fourteen? Round it up, Varma said: fifteen minutes of fame. X is the Warhol, after Andy Warhol’s line that everyone in the world will be famous for fifteen minutes.
~ Shah struck back: what is a millihelen? Helen’s was the beauty that launched a thousand ships, so a millihelen is the beauty that will launch one ship. “Nice one,” said Varma. {060-J08}
stories.why: Varma’s idea of quizzing: a question you either know or don’t is “damn boring” for people who aren’t into trivia. A good one rewards reasoning over recall, so that anyone with a mental calculator can play.

stories.start: I think this is a good frame in context beyond countries and firms
stories.end: for living one's life and thinking about what rules do I live by
stories.caption: his rules for living
stories.kicker: Amit Varma applies rules versus deals to his own life
stories.head: House rules for one
body: Rules versus deals, Amit Varma said, is a useful frame beyond countries and firms. Handling people person by person takes a lot of cognitive energy and leads to mistakes, so he sets himself rules. {060-S02}
The first: avoid negativity. A new acquaintance who complains about others and takes a victimhood attitude instead of a can-do one is best avoided, in real life and on Twitter.

The second concerns only his own behaviour: listen, try to figure out the other person’s story, and do not make himself the centre of it. He does not always succeed. “One is male and hardwired like a male, we are the centre of the universe, but one can make an effort.” {060-J10}
~ The rules one lives by, he said, might be a subject for another episode.
stories.why: Deciding in advance how to handle a whole class of situations saves mental energy and prevents mistakes, just as, Ajay Shah argued, a state should run on rules rather than case-by-case bargains. {060-C12}

stories.start: I was in a conversation with some people and um in a group
stories.end: should be really careful with our opinions and what we opine on
stories.caption: the essay-length test
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s rule against half-baked opinions
stories.head: Argue it at length or hush
body: The halo effect, Amit Varma said, makes people assume that someone who excels in one field excels in others, as if a microbiologist could give gyan on any area of medicine. {060-C18}
So these days he gives gyan only on what he has studied well enough. Earlier that same day, in a group conversation, someone kept coming up with half-baked opinions.
Varma spontaneously laid down a rule: “If you state an opinion here, you should be able to do an essay length argument for it, otherwise don’t state it.” {060-S04}
~ It sounds a little extreme, he admitted. But there is too much cheap opinion floating around on Twitter, he said, a lot of it received wisdom or tribal allegiance.
stories.why: A filter against the halo effect and the hot take: speak only on what you have studied well enough to argue at length. People like the hosts, Varma said, should be especially careful with their opinions.

quiz.q: Which three Fs make up Amit Varma’s light triad, set against the dark triad of serial killers?
quiz.a: Firms, finance and freedom, with fallacy nominated for the dark triad instead.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, did stock prices rise during the COVID catastrophe?
quiz.a: Central banks cut rates sharply, so future cash flows were discounted at lower rates.

quiz.q: What is a Warhol, in Amit Varma’s old quiz question?
quiz.a: A unit of hype: fifteen minutes of fame, so a kilo-Warhol is 10.42 days.

quiz.q: Whose definition of the state as a monopoly of physical violence did Ajay Shah cite?
quiz.a: Max Weber’s, to show that coercion is core to what a state is.

quiz.q: Why must McDonald’s offer franchisees a standard contract, though no Article 14 binds it?
quiz.a: Deal-by-deal franchising would make the organisation fall apart in complexity and corruption.

quiz.q: In Varma’s restaurant analogy, what happens to the diner outvoted by three seafood lovers?
quiz.a: They eat seafood or go hungry, even if allergic to prawns.
